common_name: Carmine Splendor Okra (Red F1 Hybrid Okra with Edible Pink Flowers)

planting.note: Direct sow after last frost once soil is reliably above 65°F; Carmine Splendor is an early F1 hybrid that begins producing in as little as 51 days, among the fastest red-podded okra varieties available.

directions: Sow seed 1/2 to 1 inch deep in full sun after soil has warmed; stalky, upright plants stay manageable while producing heavily. Carmine Splendor is a modern F1 hybrid bred for uniform, stout, five-pointed pods that emerge deep red and soften to a lighter red-pink as they enlarge, giving a longer tender-harvest window than many older red okra types. The pale yellow, red-throated flowers are edible and often used fresh as a garnish or lightly battered and fried, in addition to the pods themselves. Harvest pods at 3-4 inches every day or two during peak summer heat, since red okra fibers up quickly once pods exceed that size.

common_name: Gold Coast Okra (Dwarf Drought- and Nematode-Tolerant Heirloom Okra)

planting.note: Direct sow after last frost when soil is warm; Gold Coast is a compact, well-branched heirloom developed at LSU that tolerates drought and root-knot nematode pressure better than most okra, making it a dependable choice for lean or sandy Gulf South soils.

directions: Direct sow 1/2 to 1 inch deep after soil has warmed, spacing plants 12-18 inches apart; Gold Coast was developed at the LSU AgCenter and selected for a compact, heavily branched habit with long petioles that make hand-harvesting easier than on tall heirloom types. The spineless, light green pods stay tender to about 6 inches and hold up well to canning and freezing. Its strong root system gives Gold Coast above-average tolerance of both drought and root-knot nematodes, two of the most common stresses on okra grown in the sandy soils of the Deep South. Because pods are slower to fiber up than many varieties, Gold Coast forgives an occasional missed picking day better than fast-maturing hybrids.

common_name: Heavy Hitter Okra (High-Yield Branching Oklahoma Heirloom Okra)

planting.note: Direct sow 1/2 inch deep after last frost once soil reaches at least 65°F; Heavy Hitter branches heavily and sets multiple pods per node, so plants need the full recommended spacing to support the heavy pod load through a long summer harvest.

directions: Sow seed directly in the garden after danger of frost has passed, spacing plants 12-18 inches apart in rows 3 feet apart. Heavy Hitter was developed by grower Ron Cook of Dry Creek Farm in Oklahoma and selected specifically for extreme productivity, with well-branched plants reaching up to 7 feet tall that can set well over 100 pods per plant across a season. Because multiple pods form at each node rather than one at a time, plants need daily or near-daily picking once production ramps up to keep pods from fibering over and to keep the heavy-bearing plant setting new fruit. This branching habit makes Heavy Hitter a strong choice for gardeners who want maximum yield from a small number of plants.

common_name: Mississippi Pinkeye Purple Hull Pea (Virus-Resistant Deep South Southern Pea)

planting.note: Direct sow after last frost once soil is reliably above 65°F; Mississippi Pinkeye is an upright, semi-bush type bred with multiple disease resistances, making it one of the more reliable purple hull peas for humid Deep South gardens.

directions: Direct sow seed 1 inch deep in rows 24-30 inches apart, thinning to 4-8 inches; like other cowpeas it fixes its own nitrogen and needs little to no supplemental fertilizer. Mississippi Pinkeye is a semi-crowder Southern pea bred with resistance to fusarium wilt, root-knot nematode, and several strains of blackeye cowpea mosaic virus, distinguishing it from older purple hull types that lack that disease package. Pods emerge light green with a distinct pink 'eye' blush, then color to deep purple at the green-shell stage, and the upright plant habit holds pods above the foliage for easier hand harvest. Shell at the purple-podded green-shell stage for fresh eating, or let pods dry fully on the vine for storage peas with the characteristic cream seed coat and maroon-pink eye.

common_name: Rouge et Noir Southern Pea (Red-and-Black Louisiana Heirloom Cowpea)

planting.note: Direct sow after last frost when soil is warm; Rouge et Noir is a sprawling bush-type Southern pea that sends out long runners, so give it room or light support even though it does not require a full trellis.

directions: Direct sow seed 1 inch deep after the soil has warmed; Rouge et Noir ('red and black') is a Louisiana heirloom Southern pea traditionally grown in Washington Parish, named for its seed color change from vivid red when freshly shelled to glossy black once fully dried. Long, slender pods up to about 10 inches hold as many as 18 seeds and can be picked young and cooked whole like a snap bean, or left to fill out for shelling and drying. The vigorous, drought-tolerant bush habit produces long running vines that sprawl well beyond the main crown, so allow generous row width or provide a low support. In Louisiana foodways this variety is traditionally simmered together with lima beans and fresh green peanuts, and the dried seed has also been roasted as a coffee substitute.

common_name: Peking Black Southern Pea (Vigorous Black-Seeded Heirloom Cowpea)

planting.note: Direct sow after last frost once soil is warm; Peking Black is a vigorous climbing type that benefits from a trellis at least 4 feet tall to keep its long vines and pods off the ground.

directions: Direct sow seed 1 inch deep and provide a trellis at least 4 feet tall, since Peking Black is a vigorous climbing Southern pea rather than a compact bush type. Vines reach about 5 feet and bear abundant 8-9 inch pods that mature to fully black, glossy seed, giving high shelled yields for drying and storage. Like other cowpeas it fixes atmospheric nitrogen and tolerates heat and drought well once established, thriving through the hottest weeks of the Southern summer that slow down snap beans and other legumes. Trellising keeps pods clean and off the soil, and also makes the long harvest season easier to manage than letting the vines sprawl.
